props.title: Creation

sections.content: Creation offers a deeply personal look at Charles Darwin's struggles while writing "On the Origin of Species," with Paul Bettany delivering a haunting performance as the naturalist torn between scientific truth and religious faith. The film shares DNA with other intimate scientific biopics like A Beautiful Mind (2001) and The Theory of Everything (2014), focusing on the human cost of groundbreaking discoveries. Director Jon Amiel crafts a psychological drama that's less about evolution itself and more about Darwin's relationship with his deeply religious wife Emma (Jennifer Connelly) and his grief over his daughter Annie's death.

sections.content: The film fits into a broader tradition of science-versus-faith narratives, alongside works like Angels & Demons (2009) and Contact (1997). But where those films often deal in broad philosophical conflicts, Creation keeps its focus intimate and domestic. The movie shares thematic territory with Inherit the Wind (1960), though it approaches evolution not through courtroom drama but through personal crisis. Darwin's hallucinations of his dead daughter Annie serve as both emotional core and metaphor for his internal religious struggle.

What sets Creation apart from other science biopics is its exploration of the intersection between scientific discovery and personal loss. Unlike The Imitation Game (2014) or Hidden Figures (2016), which focus on external obstacles and societal resistance, this film delves deep into Darwin's psychological torment. The movie's structure mirrors Darwin's theory itself - showing how small, intimate moments evolve into life-changing revelations. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Science Biopics

sections.content: The 2000s and 2010s saw a surge in sophisticated science biopics that moved beyond simple great-man narratives. Films like Creation, Kinsey (2004), and Temple Grandin (2010) examined how personal lives shaped scientific breakthroughs. This trend continued with The Current War (2017) and Radioactive (2019), showing how scientific discovery often emerges from complex personal dynamics rather than isolated genius.
